name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,148

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Queen visiting revamped Antigone production

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone's home, so the monarch's letters are placed within the others
something revamped has been remade, so the play's title letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the Sophocles tragedy, taken as written before rearranging
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual crossword queen

explanation.surface: A queen attends a newly staged production of Sophocles' Antigone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Production' looks like the theatre staging the surface describes, but it is the definition, as in the generation of electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: Generation is the act of producing something, as in power generation, so it is a synonym for production.

clue.text: "As flies to wanton boys are we to th' —" (King Lear)

definitions.text: "As flies to wanton boys are we to th' —" (King Lear)

blocks.clueFragment: "As flies to wanton boys are we to th' —"
blocks.note: the surface is a famous line of Gloucester's with its last word missing
the solver supplies the missing word from the play: the beings who kill us for their sport

explanation.walkthrough: The full line runs 'As flies to wanton boys are we to th' gods; They kill us for their sport', spoken by the blinded Gloucester in Act 4.
explanation.definitionFit: The blank stands for the deities Gloucester blames for human suffering, the missing final word of the quotation.

clue.text: New backing electrified the French Shakespeare, some say

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the word for electrified is read from right to left

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
a live wire is electrified
le is the French masculine 'the'

explanation.surface: Fresh support has electrified French Shakespeare productions, as some reports have it.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Henry Neville, a Tudor courtier and diplomat, is one of the candidates put forward by those who doubt that Shakespeare wrote his own plays; hence 'some say'.
explanation.definitionFit: A minority authorship theory holds that the courtier Henry Neville was the true author behind the plays credited to Shakespeare.

clue.text: She was his equestrian witch, a flipping pain

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the word for a pain is written backwards

blocks.note: an equestrian is a horse rider
a hag is an ugly old witch
a drag is a bore or a pain

explanation.surface: A woman complains that her horse-riding partner was a witch and a flaming nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' reads as a woman, but it is the title of the 1887 adventure novel, so 'She was his' means he wrote it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian author of King Solomon's Mines also wrote the novel She, about the immortal queen Ayesha, so She was his book.

clue.text: Edits see changes in setting of Milward's Apples

indicators.note: when the letters undergo changes they are rearranged into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged, taken as written

explanation.surface: An editor notices changes in the setting of Richard Milward's novel Apples.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Milward's 2007 debut Apples follows teenagers in Middlesbrough. TEESSIDE is the industrial region of north-east England around the River Tees.
explanation.definitionFit: Milward's novel is set in Middlesbrough, the largest town of this north-eastern English region, so the region is its setting.

clue.text: In drunken reflection, might Wilde see these sculpted men?

definitions.text: In drunken reflection, might Wilde see these sculpted men?

blocks.clueFragment: In drunken reflection, might Wilde see these
blocks.note: surface: the writer, tipsy, peering into a mirror and seeing double
setter's reading: Wilde's first name, multiplied, is also the gold statuettes of the Academy Awards

explanation.walkthrough: A drunk looking in a mirror sees several of himself; Wilde's first name in the plural is also the film industry's little gold sculpted men.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Award statuettes, nicknamed after a man's first name, are cast figures of a man, and several Wildes would be several of that first name.

clue.text: Quiet English male, one of three bros in a boat

definitions.text: one of three bros in a boat

blocks.note: sh! is a call for quiet
E is the abbreviation for English
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A reserved Englishman turns out to be one of Jerome's Three Men in a Boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrasing recalls Three Men in a Boat, but the boat is Noah's ark, and the three brothers are Noah's sons Shem, Ham and Japheth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Noah's three sons sailed with him in the ark, and this is the eldest of those brothers.

clue.text: One with hand up in champion ruminant's bottom?

definitions.text: One with hand up in champion ruminant's bottom?

indicators.note: in a down entry 'up' means read from bottom to top, so this pair is written backwards
in places the reversed pair inside the word for a champion
the bottom of a word in a down entry is its last letter

blocks.note: a hero is a champion
I is the Roman numeral one
R for right, as in right hand
the last letter of ruminant

explanation.surface: A vet with a champion cow reaches deep inside the animal's rear.
explanation.walkthrough: The I and R go in reversed, so HER(RI)O, then T. Read whole, the clue pictures a vet with an arm inside a cow: the famous Yorkshire vet-author of All Creatures Great and Small.
explanation.definitionFit: James Herriot, the pen name of a Yorkshire vet, wrote memoirs full of calving and examining cattle by hand from behind.

clue.text: One related to Emily and Anne as well as Burns?

definitions.text: One related to Emily and Anne as well as Burns?

blocks.clueFragment: One related to Emily and Anne
blocks.note: surface: Emily and Anne suggest the Brontë sisters, and Burns the Scottish poet, as if naming a literary relative
setter's reading: the author of Anne of Green Gables and Emily of New Moon shares a surname with the middle name of Mr Burns of The Simpsons

explanation.walkthrough: Emily and Anne point to the Brontës and Burns to Robert Burns; in fact they are L. M. Montgomery's heroines and Charles Montgomery Burns, the miserly plant owner in The Simpsons.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname links the Canadian novelist who created both heroines with the cartoon tycoon whose middle name it is.

clue.text: Note calm coming over keen Leeds biographer

blocks.note: D is a musical note
avid means keen
peace is calm

explanation.surface: A note of calm comes over a keen biographer of Leeds.
explanation.walkthrough: Calm comes over to follow keen. David Peace wrote The Damned Utd, a fictionalised life of Brian Clough's 44 days managing Leeds United.
explanation.definitionFit: His novel The Damned Utd is a fictional biography of Brian Clough's short reign at Leeds United, and he grew up in Yorkshire.

clue.text: Press taking a different view of noir

indicators.note: seeing something differently means reordering it, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the film genre, taken as written

explanation.surface: The newspapers revise their opinion of film noir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' reads as journalists reviewing a film genre, but it is a verb: to smooth clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To iron clothes is to press them flat with a hot appliance, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Birthday party planner or thin pedlar in play

indicators.note: letters put in play are moved about freely, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged, taken as written

explanation.surface: A children's party organiser or a skinny hawker appears in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Birthday party planner' looks like an event organiser; it is the playwright who planned, that is wrote, The Birthday Party.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nobel-winning playwright wrote The Birthday Party (1958), so he is the one who devised that party.

clue.text: Obscure book university found in empty locker

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it, so this letter goes within the others
emptying a word removes its middle, leaving only its outside letters

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for book
the first and last letters of locker
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: An obscure university book turns up in an otherwise empty locker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' reads as an adjective describing the book, but it is a verb meaning to make indistinct.
explanation.definitionFit: To blur something is to make it hazy and hard to make out, which is to obscure it.

clue.text: One after Atwood's debut browsing around a city

indicators.note: around means wrapping about, so the word for browsing encloses the other letters

blocks.note: surfing the web is browsing it
taken as written
C is an abbreviation for city

explanation.surface: Someone, after reading Atwood's first novel, browses around a city.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Atwood's debut novel was The Edible Woman (1969); her second, the one after it, was Surfacing (1972).
explanation.definitionFit: Atwood's second novel followed her debut, so it is the one after it in her bibliography.

clue.text: A novel meal that requires no dressing?

definitions.text: A novel meal that requires no dressing?

blocks.note: surface: an unusual new dish, one served without salad dressing
setter's reading: a novel whose title is a meal eaten unclothed, by William Burroughs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as new, and 'dressing' as something poured on a salad; really it is a book, and the meal is one taken without clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: William Burroughs' 1959 novel has a title naming a midday meal eaten unclothed, so no dressing is needed.

clue.text: Bruno's nurse patches up laddie in hospital department

indicators.note: patching something up remakes it, so the letters of the boy are reworked
in places the rearranged letters inside the hospital department

blocks.note: A&E, accident and emergency, is the hospital casualty department
taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: Bruno's nurse patches up a young lad in the hospital's casualty department.
explanation.walkthrough: In Iris Murdoch's Bruno's Dream, Adelaide is the maid who nurses the dying old Bruno. A&E is the British name for a hospital's emergency department.
explanation.definitionFit: Adelaide cares for the bedridden Bruno in Murdoch's novel, so she serves as his nurse.

clue.text: Theatre part that Montana Wildhack might pinch?

blocks.note: first meaning: the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream, a role in the theatre
second meaning: the rear end, which a flirtatious person might pinch

explanation.walkthrough: Montana Wildhack is the film actress Billy Pilgrim is paired with in Vonnegut's Slaughterhouse-Five, a plausible pincher of behinds.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both Shakespeare's comic weaver, a stage role, and the buttocks, a body part people pinch.

clue.text: Portly blowhard reporting seasonal workers in Texas?

indicators.note: reporting is passing on by speech, so the answer sounds like the following phrase

blocks.note: Americans call autumn the fall, so autumn workers in Texas would be fall staff

explanation.surface: A fat braggart reports on the seasonal workforce in Texas.
explanation.walkthrough: The Texas question mark flags the American word for autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Falstaff, Shakespeare's fat, boastful knight, is the archetype of the corpulent windbag.

clue.text: Some maidens ignoring one such as Iago

indicators.note: some means only part of what follows, so the letters lie inside the next words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Some young women pay no attention to a villain like Iago.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago, the schemer of Othello, holds the rank of Othello's ensign, a junior officer who carries the flag.
explanation.definitionFit: Iago is Othello's ensign, so an ensign is one of his rank, a standard-bearing junior officer.

clue.text: Strongman taking on piano tutor of Guy Mannering

indicators.note: taking something on means admitting it inside, so the strongman's name encloses the letter

blocks.note: the biblical hero of great strength
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A strongman hires a piano teacher from Scott's Guy Mannering.
explanation.walkthrough: In Walter Scott's Guy Mannering, the awkward scholar Dominie Sampson is tutor to the Bertram family.
explanation.definitionFit: Dominie Sampson, the scholarly schoolmaster of Scott's novel, works as a tutor; dominie is Scots for teacher.

clue.text: Suffragist novelist, one concerned with plot

blocks.note: first meaning: Helen Hamilton ..., American novelist and campaigner for women's votes
second meaning: someone who tends a plot of land

explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' next to 'novelist' wants to be a story's plot; here it is a patch of ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Helen Hamilton Gardener wrote novels and fought for women's suffrage; separately, the word means someone who cultivates a garden plot.

clue.text: Booker-winner McEwan brought up with Theroux?

indicators.note: in a down entry brought up means raised from bottom to top, so the first name is read backwards

blocks.note: Ian McEwan, the novelist's first name
Paul Theroux, the travel writer's first name

explanation.surface: A Booker-winner is raised in the company of Ian McEwan and Paul Theroux.
explanation.walkthrough: V. S. Naipaul won the Booker in 1971 and was famously mentor, then foe, to Paul Theroux; McEwan also won the Booker, which tempts the solver to the wrong author.
explanation.definitionFit: V. S. Naipaul won the 1971 Booker Prize for In a Free State, so he is a Booker-winner.

clue.text: "This I do vow and this shall ever be I will be true, despite thy — and thee" (Shakespeare)

definitions.text: "This I do vow and this shall ever be I will be true, despite thy — and thee" (Shakespeare)

blocks.clueFragment: "This I do vow and this shall ever be I will be true, despite thy — and thee"
blocks.note: the surface is the closing couplet of a Shakespeare sonnet with one word missing
the solver supplies the missing word: the blade that Time carries

explanation.walkthrough: Sonnet 123 defies Time: 'This I do vow and this shall ever be, / I will be true, despite thy scythe and thee.'
explanation.definitionFit: The sonnet addresses Time, traditionally pictured as an old reaper carrying a long curved blade, the missing word.

clue.text: Awful crimes, like unfinished rhymes

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its end, so the final letter of the word before is dropped
awful suggests something badly made, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then cut short

explanation.surface: Terrible offences, comparable to poems left incomplete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' reads as a link joining crimes to rhymes, but it is fodder: its last letter goes and the rest is rearranged with crimes.
explanation.definitionFit: A limerick is a five-line comic verse with an AABBA scheme, so the plural is a set of rhymes.

clue.text: Bayley's elegy was for her, but not all from Dublin?

indicators.note: not all of a word means part of it is missing, here its last letter

blocks.note: someone from Dublin is Irish

explanation.surface: John Bayley's elegy honoured a woman who was only partly from Dublin.
explanation.walkthrough: John Bayley's memoir Elegy for Iris is about his wife Iris Murdoch, who was born in Dublin; the question mark admits she was really only half Irish by upbringing.
explanation.definitionFit: Bayley wrote Elegy for Iris about his wife, the novelist Iris Murdoch, so the elegy was for her.

clue.text: One opposing taking 50% off a Huxley novel

indicators.note: taking off half means removing half the letters, leaving only the first four

blocks.note: Antic Hay is Aldous Huxley's 1923 novel

explanation.surface: Someone protests at half-price copies of a Huxley novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The eight-letter title loses its second half, leaving the first four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An anti is a person who opposes something, used as a noun for an opponent.

clue.text: He might have rhymed November with cold embers

definitions.text: He might have rhymed November with cold embers

blocks.note: N is November in the NATO phonetic alphabet
cold embers are ash

explanation.surface: A poet might have paired a winter month with the dying embers of a fire.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes Ogden Nash, the American master of strained comic rhymes, who might well have paired November with embers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogden Nash was famous for forced, comic rhymes, so an outrageous pairing like November and embers is his trademark.

clue.text: Stress with gang aboard the Hogwarts Express?

indicators.note: aboard means inside a vehicle, so the gang's letters ride within the other word

blocks.note: strain is stress
a team is a gang of workers

explanation.surface: Tension mounts as a gang boards the Hogwarts Express.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: the Hogwarts Express is one particular such vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Harry Potter books the Hogwarts Express is a scarlet locomotive powered by steam, an example of the type.

clue.text: Look for a possible bride for Tom Jones

definitions.text: a possible bride for Tom Jones

blocks.note: first meaning: to search for something

blocks.clueFragment: a possible bride for Tom Jones
blocks.note: second meaning: the rich widow Mrs Arabella ..., who proposes marriage to Fielding's hero

explanation.walkthrough: Tom Jones suggests the Welsh singer; it is Fielding's novel, in which the widow Mrs Hunt writes offering marriage, which Tom declines.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to search, and in Fielding's novel a wealthy widow of this surname proposes to the hero.

clue.text: Fill frieze with new design for film director

indicators.note: a new design rearranges the parts, so the letters are put into another order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged, taken as written

explanation.surface: A set designer fills a frieze with a new pattern for a film director.
explanation.walkthrough: Franco Zeffirelli was the Italian director of Romeo and Juliet (1968), himself trained as a stage designer.
explanation.definitionFit: Franco Zeffirelli directed films such as Romeo and Juliet and Jesus of Nazareth, so he was a film director.
